sections.COMMENTS:
An over 1,000 km-long contractional belt runs along the eastern margin of the Adriatic Sea from the Alpine domain (to the North) to the Kefallonia-Lefkada Fault (to the south). The various part of this fold-and-thrust belt are known, from north to south, as Dinarides, Albanides and Hellenides and result from the continental collision between the European and African plates. Along this margin the SW-NE convergence between the two plates exhibits a strain rate of ca. 30 nanostrain/y (Hollenstein et al., 2003; Serpelloni et al., 2005), while the periodic GPS measurements give strain rates up to 70 nanostrain/yr for the external thrusting domain (Jouanne et al., 2012).
In the area of the External Albanides exposed rocks are neritic and pelagic carbonates formed on shallow platforms and in oceanic basins during the Mesozoic and Cenozoic. The oldest rocks exposed at the surface are Permo-Triassic evaporites, which have acted as a detachment layer during recent folding and thrusting (Velaj et al., 1999). Flysch deposition and folding occurred from the Eocene onward, and the surface morphology is characterized by folds that are thought to be cored by the Permo-Triassic evaporites (Velaj et al., 1999), which are also seen to crop out as diapiric structures.
Seismicity mostly concentrates in the Albanides and Hellenides. The outer portion of these chains is partly located offshore and characterized by a number of thrust fronts that all appear to be currently active. The available focal mechanisms indicate a SW-NE maximum horizontal stress axis (Papazachos et al., 1999); reverse faulting dominates, even if some smaller strike-slip events are occasionally recorded (Vannucci et al., 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2006).
Thrust faulting occurs in the lowlands of western Albania and the Adriatic Sea. Recorded earthquakes are mostly low-angle thrusting events although some events have occurred on steeper-dipping planes (Copley et al., 2008). Earthquakes appear to be spatially correlated with anticlines that are well-expressed at the surface, suggesting that the anticlines are currently active and underlain by (possibly blind) reverse faults (Copley et al., 2008). Historical and instrumental catalogues show the occurence of M >6 earthquakes all along the coastal region (Papazachos et al., 2009).
The depth of this Source was set using seismic profile data and regional geologic considerations (e.g. Gjoka and Dulaj, 1997; Velaj, 2001; Roure et al., 2004; Aliaj et al., 2006; Nieuwald et al., 2009). The geometrical fault characteristics and kinematics were based on seismic profile and geologic data combined with earthquake data (Papazachos et al.; 1999; Aliaj et al., 2000; Roure et al., 2004; Aliaj et al., 2006; Graham Wall et al., 2006). The slip rate was inferred from geological data and regional geodynamic considerations.
We also considered the results of the seismic zonation by Aliaj et al. (2004) to the Ionian Coast Seismic Source Zone, which includes almost completely this Source.
